stories.title: Google DeepMind announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its strongest model yet, with a cautious rollout that starts with cyber defenders
paragraphs: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon on Oct. 28, 2026, calling it its next frontier model and its strongest yet, with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. In a blog post by Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect at Google, the company says Carbon builds on Gemini 4 Argon, which launched two weeks earlier, and ranks first on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59.

DeepMind says Carbon is built for sustained agentic work on hard, long-horizon engineering problems, and that internally its teams have seen it run for days to root-cause and patch subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. On cybersecurity benchmarks evaluated without guardrails, the company reports 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching. It also says Carbon more than doubles Argon's success rate at generating secure code on internal benchmarks, and gained 89 Elo points to reach fourth place (1769) on WebDev Arena.

On safety, DeepMind says Carbon uses the same layered safety stack as Argon and was trained to avoid shortcuts: it reports that successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, high-severity misalignment alerts in live internal coding dropped by almost 80%, unsupported claims fell by about half compared with Argon, and the attack success rate on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark was 0.0%.

The rollout is deliberately limited. DeepMind says it is taking part in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing process, and that starting this week Carbon will go to a subset of cyber defenders, with access phased in to more trusted partners through its Fairwind Program before it reaches developers, businesses and consumers. Introductory pricing matches Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4 and $20 after the introductory period, according to the post.

stories.title: Google DeepMind unveils Genie 4, a world model that generates interactive scenes with sound and can be steered in real time
paragraphs: Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, its new world model, on Oct. 27, 2026, in a blog post by Raia Hadsell, Diego Rivas and Hang Qi. The company says the model brings more realistic, real-time interactive simulation and is natively multimodal, generating music, ambient noise and interactive dialogue at the same time as the world itself. It succeeds Genie 3, which DeepMind announced as a research preview in August 2025.

According to DeepMind, Genie 4 builds on the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models handle the reasoning that keeps a simulation coherent. Users move through a world with keyboard controls and can type plain-language prompts mid-session to change the weather, move the camera or add a new person or object, and Gemini adapts the prompt to fit the scene. MarkTechPost reports that Gemini 3.8 Flash plans a goal as a series of steps and checks incoming frames to confirm each one worked, and TechCrunch reports that Genie 4 can keep a scene consistent for up to two minutes, double its predecessor's limit.

DeepMind says simulating the world is a crucial part of building AGI and that Genie 4 could help create training environments for robots and agents. TechCrunch and MarkTechPost describe a research experiment tied to Gemini Robotics in which a Gemini 4 Argon model broke a task into steps that Genie 4 simulated in real time; MarkTechPost says the demo showed Apptronik's Apollo humanoid playing checkers. TechCrunch also notes the team acknowledged gaps: details and objects can drift the longer a simulation runs, and audio accuracy and legible in-world text are not yet solved.

Genie 4 is available now as a research preview for trusted testers. DeepMind says it will then reach Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, and TechCrunch reports that rollout is expected in the coming weeks. MarkTechPost reports that all Genie 4 video and audio will carry SynthID watermarks and that DeepMind released no benchmark tables for the model.

stories.title: Artemis I data show radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but by less than expected
paragraphs: Radiation detectors that flew around the Moon on NASA's uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022 have produced new preliminary measurements of cosmic radiation near the Moon, according to a ScienceDaily release from the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) dated Oct. 28, 2026. The Orion spacecraft carried more than 10,000 tiny crystals inside two human-shaped mannequins as part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study. The results were published in the journal Radiation Measurements in a paper led by Paweł Bilski of IFJ PAN.

The release says total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than in low Earth orbit because of galactic radiation, but the difference is not as large as one might expect. Bilski explains that low-energy protons trapped in Earth's Van Allen belts can make up most of the dose astronauts receive in low Earth orbit, and that contribution disappears near the Moon. High-energy galactic particles can pass through the entire body, so the Artemis I detectors recorded doses spread almost evenly through the mannequins, unlike the uneven pattern seen in the earlier MATROSHKA experiment on the International Space Station.

The study also tested a new kind of passive detector: millimeter-sized lithium fluoride crystals that record the tracks of charged particles and can be read with a fluorescence microscope. Universe Today reports that traditional plastic detectors must be etched in hot sodium hydroxide before they can be read, which destroys them and creates hazardous waste. According to IFJ PAN, after corrections and new background-removal software, the crystal results differed by no more than 15% from conventional track detectors across the overlapping range, and they also picked up many particle tracks below the older detectors' threshold.

Universe Today adds that for the highest energy transfers, the new sensors overestimated the dose by around 30% compared with the plastic detectors, which the researchers suspect comes from secondary neutrons knocking lithium atoms out of place inside the crystal. The team used crystals enriched in lithium-7 to reduce those reactions. IFJ PAN says the detectors are small enough to be worn by people, making them practical for monitoring astronaut radiation exposure on future missions.

stories.title: Heat deaths linked to climate change hit a record high, and Lancet Countdown researchers call for a global health emergency
paragraphs: Researchers behind The Lancet's 2026 Countdown on Health and Climate Change are calling for climate change to be formally recognized as a global health emergency, ScienceAlert reported Oct. 27, 2026. The report finds that risks and harms tied to extreme heat and drought are rising faster than climate action, despite a decade of growing investment in moving away from fossil fuels. It comes 10 years after the first Countdown report and tracks the effects of climate change on 54 health indicators.

"Heat deaths linked to climate change have reached a record-high," said Marina Romanello, executive director of The Lancet Countdown. According to the report's estimates, as reported by ScienceAlert, 71.5% of heat-related deaths worldwide in 2023 can be attributed to climate change: about 710,000 deaths, compared with around 200,000 without it. From 2016 to 2023, an estimated 540,800 deaths a year were linked to heat, and climate change was responsible for 68% of them, up from 55% a year in 2006 to 2015.

The report puts the cost of heat to global economic productivity in 2025 at about $1.07 trillion, just from interrupting people's ability to work, with the biggest losses in the economies of Southeast Asia and Africa. Agriculture and construction were hit especially hard because they rely on demanding outdoor work. Romanello said drought is also spreading while other places flood, and ScienceAlert notes the report finds the world's 100 largest oil and gas companies plan, by 2040, to exceed by 150% the fossil fuel production that would be consistent with keeping warming below 1.5°C.

The authors say the World Health Organization and United Nations should declare a global health emergency, put health at the center of climate decisions and increase grant-based funding for climate and health work. Co-chair Anthony Costello said health-centered climate action, such as cleaner air and better warning systems, is already saving lives, "but the pace and scale of emissions reduction remains entirely out of step with the pace and scale of the harm."

stories.title: Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate, an icy world beyond Pluto called 2026 ED138
paragraphs: Scientists have found a distant, icy body orbiting beyond Pluto that may be added to the solar system's official list of dwarf planets, according to a University of Washington release published on Phys.org on Oct. 27, 2026. The object, provisionally named 2026 ED138, was spotted earlier this month in data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The results were presented at a press conference on Oct. 27 by Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics who first spotted the object, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team.

According to the release, initial measurements place ED138 among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. "Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."

Holman found the object on the evening of Oct. 13 by running Rubin data through a search code he developed with colleague Kevin Napier, which compares billions of detections of moving objects to find the ones that belong to the same body. Jurić then found 20 more Rubin observations going back to March 2026, and the team also spotted ED138 in archival images from other surveys going back to 2016, giving them more than 10 years of its orbit. The release says the object sits in a crowded region of sky near the plane of the Milky Way, which is likely why it went unnoticed until now.

ED138 is currently about 46 astronomical units from the sun, compared with Pluto's average distance of 40 au. Based on its distance, brightness and estimated surface reflectivity, the team estimates it is between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (370 and 930 miles) across, and the release notes that icy bodies this large are expected to be round, one of the requirements for a dwarf planet. Further observations are needed to measure its exact size and confirm that it is a dwarf planet. The discovery follows Rubin's announcement in April of more than 11,000 new asteroids, including roughly 380 new trans-Neptunian objects, before its Legacy Survey of Space and Time formally began in June 2026.

stories.title: Anthropic files to go public, with plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT
paragraphs: Anthropic announced on Oct. 26, 2026, that it has filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock. The company says it intends to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT," and that the number of shares to be offered and the price range have not yet been determined. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are named as the lead underwriters.

According to CNBC's coverage of the filing, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.29 billion for the six months ended June 30, 2026, up 1,304% from $1.16 billion a year earlier, and $4.59 billion in revenue for all of 2025. It reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of 2026, which the company says largely reflects accounting charges from changes in the value of convertible notes tied to increases in its valuation. CNBC reports that consumption-based revenue made up 80% of the total in that period and subscriptions 20%.

CNBC reports that the filing describes a governance structure Anthropic says has "no direct public company precedent." A company called Founder LLC, whose sole members are Anthropic's seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, will hold 50.1% of the voting power of outstanding shares. Anthropic says in the filing that the structure may make it more difficult to replace its directors and management and is likely to limit the chance of an unsolicited takeover.

CNBC reports the filing lists 5,300 employees as of Sept. 30, more than 11,900 enterprise customers with at least $100,000 in trailing-twelve-month revenue, and more than 90 pages of risk factors, including AI safety, dependence on TSMC for chips, and data center construction moratoriums. The filing names OpenAI and Google as its direct competitors and, according to CNBC, describes a compute agreement with SpaceX of up to $120.5 billion running into 2029. Anthropic says no sales can take place until the registration statement becomes effective.
